items.title: Ken Poston interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2024
items.q: Jay and I went to lunch about once a week when I was working at the Kansas City Jazz Commission.

ctx.x: Count Basie was coming to Kansas City and because we had played all those Sammy Nestico charts in the high school band, I knew who — Count Basie, I’d read about Count Basie and the connection to Kansas City that I thought for the school newspaper I was going to write a big history of Kansas City jazz and this would be great if I could interview Count Basie then that could be a part of my Kansas City jazz history and it’d be really great in high school to be able to do that. So our principal knew somebody and was…

which I heard him do many other times but I didn’t know this at the time but I heard him do this in many other interviews, “Oh well you see I’m writing a book. I’m writing my biography, and I can’t talk about those things that are going to be in the book, so you got any more questions? And of course you can imagine like a 16-, 17-year-old kid that has — and I don’t know what to do. So I kind of re-phrased the question. I guess I don’t know what I said but I kind of re-phrased it. And then Basie goes, “You know…

a younger woman, comes over to Jay and she says, “I know you. My mom has all your records. I know you, you’re famous.” And Jay, you know, you know Jay, Jay was real humble and you know Jay’s like, “Oh well.” “Yeah, yeah, I know who you are. My mom has all your records. I grew up listening to you.” And Jay’s like, “Oh.” She goes, “You’re Bobby Blue Bland.” And so Jay starts trying to convince her that he’s not. And I’m just sitting there cracking up you know. And Jay’s like, “No, no, my name’s Jay.” And she’s…
